rules.title: Restricted or server-only secret is hardcoded in the app
rules.why: Anything in the app can be extracted by anyone who downloads it. A cloud key, model-provider key, payment key, repository token, or private key found this way lets an attacker spend your money or act as your servers.
rules.fix: Rotate the credential first, because it is already exposed. Then move the call behind your backend so the key never ships, and read server-side keys from your CI or server secret store.
rules.verify: Run `strings` on the release APK or IPA and search for the key's prefix; nothing should come back. Turn on push protection or a secret scanner so a new key can't be committed.

rules.title: Google API key in code (restrict it in the console)
rules.why: Maps and Firebase keys are client identifiers: they ship in every app and anyone can read them. Without restrictions, someone else can use your key and your quota.
rules.fix: In Google Cloud Console, restrict the key to your Android package name and signing certificate, or your iOS bundle ID, and to only the APIs it needs. If it calls a paid API such as Gemini, move that call behind your backend instead.
rules.verify: In Google Cloud Console, open the key's page and confirm it lists application restrictions and API restrictions.

rules.title: Client or API secret is assigned a literal value
rules.why: A value named as a secret ships inside the app, where anyone can extract it. An OAuth client secret in a mobile app protects nothing and lets others impersonate your app to the server.
rules.fix: Rotate the secret. Mobile OAuth clients should use PKCE with no client secret; other secrets belong on your backend. If the value is not a secret, rename it so reviewers can tell.
rules.verify: Search the release build with `strings` for the value; it should be gone.

rules.title: AES in ECB mode, or with no mode named
rules.why: ECB encrypts identical blocks to identical ciphertext, so patterns in the data show through, and it detects no tampering. On Android, `Cipher.getInstance("AES")` with no mode can silently give you ECB.
rules.fix: Use AES-GCM (`AES/GCM/NoPadding`) with a Keystore key, or Tink's AEAD, or CryptoKit's `AES.GCM` on iOS. Re-encrypt existing data under the new scheme.
rules.verify: Search for `AES/ECB`, `"AES"`, and `kCCOptionECBMode`; every remaining hit should be gone or explained in a comment.

fix_code.code:
import javax.crypto.Cipher
import javax.crypto.SecretKey
import javax.crypto.spec.GCMParameterSpec

private const val IV_BYTES = 12
private const val TAG_BITS = 128

fun encrypt(plaintext: ByteArray, key: SecretKey, aad: ByteArray): ByteArray {
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.ENCRYPT_MODE, key)          // the Keystore generates the IV; do not supply one
    cipher.updateAAD(aad)                          // e.g. "refresh_token", binds purpose to ciphertext
    val ciphertext = cipher.doFinal(plaintext)
    return cipher.iv + ciphertext                  // store the IV alongside; it is not secret
}

fun decrypt(stored: ByteArray, key: SecretKey, aad: ByteArray): ByteArray {
    val iv = stored.copyOfRange(0, IV_BYTES)
    val ciphertext = stored.copyOfRange(IV_BYTES, stored.size)
    val cipher = Cipher.getInstance("AES/GCM/NoPadding")
    cipher.init(Cipher.DECRYPT_MODE, key, GCMParameterSpec(TAG_BITS, iv))
    cipher.updateAAD(aad)
    return cipher.doFinal(ciphertext)              // throws AEADBadTagException if tampered
}

rules.title: AES-CBC needs a separate MAC to detect tampering
rules.why: CBC hides data but doesn't detect changes. An attacker can alter ciphertext to change the plaintext predictably, and padding errors can leak the plaintext byte by byte.
rules.fix: Prefer AES-GCM. If you must keep CBC, compute an HMAC-SHA-256 over the IV and the ciphertext with a separate key, and check it in constant time before decrypting.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm a MAC over IV plus ciphertext is checked before decryption, or that the code moved to GCM.

rules.title: Fixed IV or nonce
rules.why: An IV or nonce must be fresh for every message. With GCM, one repeat under the same key reveals the XOR of the two plaintexts and lets an attacker forge messages.
rules.fix: Don't supply an IV. Let the Keystore, Tink, or CryptoKit generate a random 12-byte nonce for each encryption, and store it next to the ciphertext.
rules.verify: For each encryption call, confirm the IV comes from `cipher.iv` after `init`, or from a secure random source, never from a constant.

fix_code.code:
import javax.crypto.Cipher

rules.title: MD5 or SHA-1 used (fine only as a non-security checksum)
rules.why: Attackers can build two different inputs with the same MD5 or SHA-1 hash. Anything that relies on these hashes for integrity, signatures, or identity can be forged.
rules.fix: Use SHA-256 or stronger. If the hash is only a non-security checksum, such as detecting a corrupted download, add a comment saying so.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm it uses SHA-256 or is commented as a non-security checksum.

rules.title: Non-cryptographic or seeded random number generator
rules.why: Default random generators are built for speed, not unpredictability: an attacker can often predict later values from a few samples. A seeded generator repeats its values for anyone who can guess the seed.
rules.fix: For keys, nonces, salts, and tokens, use `SecureRandom()` with the default constructor on Android and `SecRandomCopyBytes` on iOS, and never seed them. Other uses, such as shuffling a list for display, are fine.
rules.verify: For each hit, confirm the value doesn't protect anything, or that it now comes from `SecureRandom` or `SecRandomCopyBytes`.

rules.title: Hardcoded plain-HTTP URL
rules.why: Anyone on the same network, such as public Wi-Fi, can read and change plain HTTP traffic. Even if the platform blocks cleartext today, an exception added later would let this URL through.
rules.fix: Change the URL to `https://`. If the server doesn't support HTTPS, fix the server; don't add a cleartext exception.
rules.verify: Build a release version and confirm requests to this host use HTTPS, or fail with a cleartext error.

rules.title: Token, password, or secret written to the log
rules.why: A token in a log line is a token on disk. Logs reach `adb logcat`, bug reports, and crash reporters that upload recent lines.
rules.fix: Remove the value from the message. Plant a release logging tree that drops everything below error, and strip `Log.v/d/i` with R8's `-assumenosideeffects`. On iOS, remove debug logging from release builds; where a log line stays, use `Logger` and leave dynamic values at the default `.private` privacy, never `privacy: .public` for a token.
rules.verify: Install a release build, sign in, and watch `adb logcat` (or Console.app on iOS): no token or password should appear.

rules.title: Encryption key is hardcoded in the app
rules.why: Anything in the app package is public. A key written in the code can be read from the APK or IPA in minutes, and then every copy of the encrypted data can be decrypted. It also can't be rotated without an app update.
rules.fix: Generate the key on the device inside the Android Keystore or the iOS Keychain or Secure Enclave, and never export it. Tink with a Keystore-protected keyset does this for you. If a server must decrypt, wrap a random per-session key with the server's public key instead of sharing one symmetric key.
rules.verify: For every `SecretKeySpec(`, `SymmetricKey(data:`, and `Key.from…(` call, confirm the key bytes come from the Keystore, the Keychain, Tink, or a secure random source, never from a string or byte literal.
